value.name: Data-center VXLAN overlay pattern
steps: VM or cluster endpoint emits packet
VXLAN encapsulates the inner Ethernet frame
IP underlay routes encapsulated packet
remote VXLAN endpoint decapsulates
destination VM or cluster receives frame
value.grounding: General technical illustration consistent with the article's VXLAN/data-center discussion; exact implementation details are model-expanded.

value.name: Provider BGP VPN WAN pattern
steps: Enterprise sites connect to provider edge
Provider uses BGP VPN mechanisms to maintain isolated routing context
Provider infrastructure transports traffic across WAN
Remote site receives traffic in its enterprise routing context
value.grounding: Illustrative generalization of the article's BGP VPN use case; specific control-plane details vary by implementation.

value.name: Resilient overlay path recovery pattern
steps: RON nodes measure path quality among participating nodes
A direct path degrades or disconnects
Overlay compares direct and relay paths against application-specific metrics
Traffic is rerouted directly or through another RON node
Node continues monitoring for future path changes
value.grounding: Based on the article's RON section.

value.name: End-system multicast delivery pattern
steps: Source publishes stream or data
Peers form an overlay distribution topology
Each overlay edge uses an underlying unicast path
Peers forward data to downstream peers
Topology is maintained as participants or paths change
value.grounding: Based on the article's overlay multicast section.

value.name: Logical-address DHT lookup pattern
steps: Application has a logical key or destination identifier
DHT routes lookup across overlay nodes
Responsible node is discovered without requester knowing its IP beforehand
Application sends message using discovered overlay route
value.grounding: Based on the article's DHT discussion; exact lookup procedure depends on the DHT algorithm.

overlay_families.description: Encapsulation/tunnel-based approaches that create logical connectivity over an underlay.
Provider and enterprise WAN overlays, including VPN and programmable SD-WAN approaches.
Overlays that organize peers or route using logical identifiers rather than only destination IP addresses.
Peer-based distribution over underlying unicast paths.
Systems named by the article among overlay networks; this grouping is a taxonomy aid and does not imply identical designs or guarantees.

value.benefit: Can identify and route to destinations independently of their currently known IP address.
value.cost_or_limit: Requires overlay-level naming, lookup, or routing mechanisms.

value.benefit: Can select overlay-node sequence and apply application/site/user-specific policies.
value.cost_or_limit: Cannot directly control the underlay's route between two overlay nodes.

value.benefit: Can detect path degradation and reroute at the overlay layer.
value.cost_or_limit: Still depends on lower-layer availability and may choose a longer path.

value.benefit: Can provide logical isolation and optionally encryption.
value.cost_or_limit: An overlay by itself does not guarantee confidentiality, authentication, or secure endpoint behavior.

value.benefit: Enables logical networks and tunnels over shared infrastructure.
value.cost_or_limit: Additional headers consume capacity and can affect MTU/fragmentation behavior (MTU note is model-expanded).

value.benefit: Can prioritize traffic by application, user, or site.
value.cost_or_limit: DiffServ prioritization does not itself guarantee end-to-end throughput.

value.benefit: Can distribute data among peers without relying on router-level IP multicast.
value.cost_or_limit: Requires maintaining an overlay topology and may create redundant transmissions.

records.title: Proof of Work — Full Detail Knowledge Graph

value.title: Proof of Work — Full Detail Knowledge Graph
value.description: Machine-readable knowledge graph covering proof-of-work fundamentals, history, algorithms, consensus, mining, security, economics, environmental considerations, useful-work variants, people and publications from the supplied article.

value.name: Hashcash anti-spam stamp
value.description: Require a sender to generate a hash satisfying a recipient- or message-bound difficulty target, then verify it cheaply before accepting the request.

steps.action: Construct a stamp from version, difficulty, date, resource identifier and trial value.
effects: stamp binds work to the request context

steps.action: Search candidate values until the stamp hash meets the leading-zero target.
Attach the stamp to the request or email.
Verify the stamp hash and target with a small number of computations.
effects: request can be accepted or rejected based on policy

value.name: Bitcoin-style proof-of-work mining loop
value.description: Miners search over candidate block data and trial values until a digest satisfies the network difficulty target; nodes independently validate the result.

steps.action: Assemble a candidate block template.
effects: candidate transactions and metadata are selected

steps.action: Vary nonce or other candidate data and compute SHA-256-based hashes.
Check each digest against the difficulty target.
Broadcast a candidate block when a valid proof is found.
effects: other nodes can inspect the candidate

steps.action: Nodes validate proof, transactions and consensus rules.
effects: valid block may extend the canonical chain

steps.action: Miner may receive the block reward if the block is accepted.

value.name: Merchant confirmation risk management
value.description: Use increasing confirmation depth as a practical way to increase the computational burden of reversing a payment, while recognizing that confirmations are not absolute finality.

steps.action: Observe the block containing the payment transaction.
Wait for additional blocks to build on that block.
Evaluate transaction value and network risk before releasing goods or services.
Avoid treating a fixed number of confirmations as a mathematical guarantee against all attacks.

value.name: Difficulty adjustment to target block interval
value.description: Periodically change the proof threshold based on observed block production to keep average production near a target interval.

steps.action: Measure block production over the protocol's adjustment window.
Compare observed timing with the target interval.
effects: direction and magnitude of adjustment are determined

steps.action: Update the difficulty parameter under consensus rules.
Nodes enforce the same adjustment rules.
effects: consensus remains deterministic across compliant nodes

value.name: Coordinated mining pool
value.description: Miners coordinate work through a pool to smooth reward variance and divide payouts, while creating concentration and coordination considerations.

steps.action: Miners contribute hash power to a pool.
Pool distributes candidate work or assignments.
effects: participants search for valid proof candidates

steps.action: Pool accounts for submitted work and accepted blocks.
effects: contribution and reward shares can be calculated

steps.action: Monitor pool concentration and operational control.

value.name: Proof of useful work optimization loop
value.description: Combine a consensus protocol with a computational task whose output can solve an optimization problem beyond producing a proof.

steps.action: Define a useful optimization problem and verifiable solution criteria.
Run the selected local-search or optimization algorithm.
Verify solution validity and protocol eligibility.
effects: valid work can contribute to consensus

steps.action: Apply the protocol's consensus and reward rules.
effects: participants are incentivized for useful computation

value.name: Optimisable proof-of-work algorithm market
value.description: Reward both problem solvers and contributors of improved algorithms according to adoption and a proportional influence mechanism.

steps.action: Specify a family of computational challenges.
effects: multiple problem classes can be used

steps.action: Contributors submit improved algorithms.
Miners select and run algorithms to solve challenge instances.
effects: algorithm adoption and performance become observable

steps.action: Calculate influence and distribute rewards under protocol rules.
effects: solvers and algorithm contributors can be compensated

value.name: Proof-of-work security-budget review
value.description: Assess whether the resources securing a network remain adequate relative to plausible attack resources and economic incentives.

steps.action: Estimate honest network hash rate and its concentration.
Estimate the cost and availability of acquiring attack hash power.
Review subsidy, fees, energy costs, hardware access and pool concentration.
Model reorganization, censorship and double-spend consequences.
Reassess after reward changes, halvings or market shifts.
effects: security assumptions are revisited over time

value.name: Energy-aware and interruptible mining operations
value.description: Where market and grid conditions permit, treat mining as a controllable load while evaluating energy source and external costs.

steps.action: Measure electricity use and the energy supply mix.
Identify contractual and technical ability to curtail load.
Respond to grid or market signals where safe and permitted.
Report environmental assumptions and limitations transparently.
effects: externalities are not hidden behind simple energy-price comparisons

value.name: PoW client puzzle for abusive request control
value.description: Use adaptive challenge difficulty to raise the cost of abusive high-volume requests while keeping legitimate traffic usable.

steps.action: Observe service load and abuse indicators.
effects: current risk and capacity are assessed

steps.action: Issue a challenge with a policy-selected difficulty.
effects: requester must perform bounded or probabilistic work

steps.action: Verify the response cheaply.
effects: valid proof can be checked with low server effort

steps.action: Combine PoW with conventional abuse controls and accessibility safeguards.
effects: PoW is not treated as a complete standalone defense

value.name: Chain reorganization response
value.description: Handle competing chain history by applying protocol rules consistently and treating transaction reversals as a risk requiring operational awareness.

steps.action: Detect that a competing chain conflicts with previously accepted blocks.
Validate competing blocks and their proof under consensus rules.
Follow the protocol's canonical-chain selection rule.
effects: nodes converge on the accepted chain under normal assumptions

steps.action: Notify affected services about transactions removed or replaced by the reorganization.

value.title: Proof generation should be costly relative to verification
value.statement: A PoW design should document the prover's expected work factor and verifier's validation cost; a high prover cost without cheap reliable verification defeats the core asymmetry.

value.title: Difficulty controls expected work, not the meaning of the result
value.statement: Difficulty should be selected for the threat model and service context; satisfying a target proves compliance with that target, not that arbitrary useful work was performed.

value.title: Interactive challenges can adapt to service load
value.statement: Where challenge-response is used, adapt difficulty carefully so abuse becomes expensive without making legitimate requests impractical.

value.title: Bind anti-spam work to the request context
value.statement: A Hashcash-style stamp should be checked against its specified fields and policy to reduce trivial replay or cross-context reuse.

value.title: Nodes must independently validate candidate blocks
value.statement: A miner's claim is not sufficient; nodes must verify proof validity, transactions and consensus rules before accepting a block.

value.title: Confirmations increase confidence but are not absolute finality
value.statement: Operational payment policies should account for value and reorganization risk rather than treating any fixed confirmation count as impossible to reverse.

value.title: Majority hash power can reorganize history
value.statement: Threat models should include reorganization, double spending and censorship when an attacker controls a majority of relevant mining power.

value.title: Monitor miner revenue as a security input
value.statement: Track subsidy and fees alongside hash rate, energy and hardware economics; lower rewards can alter the cost of attacking the network.

value.title: Measure mining concentration, not only total hash rate
value.statement: Total network hash rate does not by itself reveal how mining power is coordinated or controlled; monitor pools and ownership concentration.

value.title: ASIC resistance is not equivalent to attack resistance
value.statement: Commodity-hardware designs may lower specialization advantages while making large amounts of rentable general-purpose compute relevant to attack analysis.

value.title: Report energy consumption with context
value.statement: Energy assessments should state the measurement period, energy mix, system boundary and assumptions; electricity use alone does not settle all environmental or grid questions.

value.title: Useful-work consensus requires verifiable task outputs
value.statement: PoUW needs task definitions and solution checks that are compatible with decentralized validation and the consensus security model.

value.title: Specify reward attribution for algorithm contributions
value.statement: OPoW-style systems need transparent influence and reward rules so miners and algorithm contributors can understand how adoption affects compensation.

value.title: Memory-bound work shifts rather than eliminates hardware economics
value.statement: Memory-intensive algorithms can alter hardware advantages, but implementation, memory bandwidth, ASIC development and access to hardware still require analysis.

value.title: Treat article-specific statistics and estimates as source-reported
value.statement: Time-bound attack-cost estimates, energy estimates, policy status and adoption statistics should be revalidated before operational or financial decisions.

value.title: PoW should not be treated as a complete DoS defense
value.statement: Computational puzzles can raise abuse cost but should be evaluated alongside rate limits, authentication, queueing and accessibility constraints.

value.title: Network value does not itself guarantee adequate security expenditure
value.statement: Compare the resources protecting a network with plausible attack costs; a large market capitalization alone does not establish that history is expensive to rewrite.

value.title: Difficulty adjustment must be deterministic across compliant nodes
value.statement: Every node should apply the same protocol rules and input window when deriving the updated target to avoid consensus divergence.

value.title: Verify a Hashcash-style anti-spam stamp
value.scenario: A service wants to impose a computational cost on high-volume requests.
steps: Select a difficulty policy appropriate to the service and request context.
Have the client search for a stamp whose SHA-1 digest satisfies the stated leading-zero requirement, if reproducing the historical example.
Verify the supplied stamp and its bound fields.
Reject invalid or policy-expired stamps and apply ordinary abuse controls as well.
value.outcome: The service can impose asymmetric computational cost, while recognizing that PoW is only one abuse-control mechanism.

value.title: Simplified proof-of-work mining flow
value.scenario: A miner participates in a Bitcoin-style proof-of-work network.
steps: Build a candidate block template from candidate transactions and metadata.
Repeatedly vary nonce or other eligible candidate data and compute SHA-256-based hashes.
Compare each result with the network's target.
Broadcast a candidate only after a valid proof is found.
Nodes independently verify the proof and all consensus rules.
value.outcome: A valid candidate may extend the chain and earn a block reward if accepted; this is a conceptual workflow, not production mining software.

value.title: Choose a merchant confirmation policy
value.scenario: A merchant receives a cryptocurrency payment and needs a practical settlement policy.
steps: Assess transaction value and the consequences of reversal.
Observe the transaction's block confirmation.
Wait for additional blocks according to the merchant's risk policy.
Reassess chain health and relevant attack conditions before releasing high-value goods.
value.outcome: The merchant makes an explicit risk-based decision rather than assuming one confirmation guarantees irreversibility.

value.title: Review a PoW network's security budget
value.scenario: A protocol team wants to understand whether miner incentives remain sufficient as subsidy changes.
steps: Track block subsidy and transaction fees over time.
Estimate network hash rate and concentration among pools or operators.
Assess hardware and energy costs and the availability of rentable hash power.
Compare plausible attack resources with the network's protection and economic exposure.
Repeat after halvings or material market changes.
value.outcome: The team has a structured threat and economic review; numerical estimates must use current, independently verified data.

value.title: Use a verifiable SAT task as useful work
value.scenario: A research protocol explores using a Boolean optimization problem in a PoUW design.
steps: Define a SAT instance and a machine-checkable solution criterion.
Run a search algorithm such as a WalkSAT variant to produce candidate assignments.
Verify the candidate independently.
Integrate accepted work only according to the protocol's consensus and reward rules.
value.outcome: The computation may contribute to an optimization task while still requiring careful design of verification, incentives and consensus safety.

value.title: Reward algorithm improvement in OPoW
value.scenario: A protocol wants to incentivize both solving challenge instances and improving the algorithms used to solve them.
steps: Define eligible computational challenge classes and validity checks.
Allow contributors to submit improved algorithms.
Measure adoption and apply the published influence calculation.
Distribute rewards to solvers and contributors according to transparent rules.
value.outcome: The system attempts to reward useful algorithmic improvement without conflating every solution with block creation.

value.title: Evaluate interruptible mining load
value.scenario: A mining operator evaluates whether its electricity load can provide demand-response value.
steps: Measure load and document the electricity supply mix.
Determine whether the site can safely and contractually curtail consumption.
Evaluate grid signals, market rules and operational constraints.
Report both energy impacts and the limits of the analysis.
value.outcome: The operator can assess possible grid flexibility without claiming that all mining is renewable or environmentally beneficial.

value.title: Evaluate an ASIC-resistant algorithm trade-off
value.scenario: A protocol designer wants mining to remain feasible on commodity hardware.
steps: Benchmark representative CPU and GPU implementations.
Assess memory, bandwidth, energy and software implementation costs.
Estimate the availability and cost of rented commodity compute.
Model majority-attack and centralization scenarios.
Document the trade-off instead of treating ASIC resistance as a security guarantee.
value.outcome: The design review distinguishes access goals from actual network attack resistance.

architecture_patterns.name: Hashcash anti-spam stamp
architecture_patterns.description: Require a sender to generate a hash satisfying a recipient- or message-bound difficulty target, then verify it cheaply before accepting the request.

steps.action: Construct a stamp from version, difficulty, date, resource identifier and trial value.
effects: stamp binds work to the request context

steps.action: Search candidate values until the stamp hash meets the leading-zero target.
Attach the stamp to the request or email.
Verify the stamp hash and target with a small number of computations.
effects: request can be accepted or rejected based on policy

architecture_patterns.name: Bitcoin-style proof-of-work mining loop
architecture_patterns.description: Miners search over candidate block data and trial values until a digest satisfies the network difficulty target; nodes independently validate the result.

steps.action: Assemble a candidate block template.
effects: candidate transactions and metadata are selected

steps.action: Vary nonce or other candidate data and compute SHA-256-based hashes.
Check each digest against the difficulty target.
Broadcast a candidate block when a valid proof is found.
effects: other nodes can inspect the candidate

steps.action: Nodes validate proof, transactions and consensus rules.
effects: valid block may extend the canonical chain

steps.action: Miner may receive the block reward if the block is accepted.

architecture_patterns.name: Merchant confirmation risk management
architecture_patterns.description: Use increasing confirmation depth as a practical way to increase the computational burden of reversing a payment, while recognizing that confirmations are not absolute finality.

steps.action: Observe the block containing the payment transaction.
Wait for additional blocks to build on that block.
Evaluate transaction value and network risk before releasing goods or services.
Avoid treating a fixed number of confirmations as a mathematical guarantee against all attacks.

architecture_patterns.name: Difficulty adjustment to target block interval
architecture_patterns.description: Periodically change the proof threshold based on observed block production to keep average production near a target interval.

steps.action: Measure block production over the protocol's adjustment window.
Compare observed timing with the target interval.
effects: direction and magnitude of adjustment are determined

steps.action: Update the difficulty parameter under consensus rules.
Nodes enforce the same adjustment rules.
effects: consensus remains deterministic across compliant nodes

architecture_patterns.name: Coordinated mining pool
architecture_patterns.description: Miners coordinate work through a pool to smooth reward variance and divide payouts, while creating concentration and coordination considerations.

steps.action: Miners contribute hash power to a pool.
Pool distributes candidate work or assignments.
effects: participants search for valid proof candidates

steps.action: Pool accounts for submitted work and accepted blocks.
effects: contribution and reward shares can be calculated

steps.action: Monitor pool concentration and operational control.

architecture_patterns.name: Proof of useful work optimization loop
architecture_patterns.description: Combine a consensus protocol with a computational task whose output can solve an optimization problem beyond producing a proof.

steps.action: Define a useful optimization problem and verifiable solution criteria.
Run the selected local-search or optimization algorithm.
Verify solution validity and protocol eligibility.
effects: valid work can contribute to consensus

steps.action: Apply the protocol's consensus and reward rules.
effects: participants are incentivized for useful computation

architecture_patterns.name: Optimisable proof-of-work algorithm market
architecture_patterns.description: Reward both problem solvers and contributors of improved algorithms according to adoption and a proportional influence mechanism.

steps.action: Specify a family of computational challenges.
effects: multiple problem classes can be used

steps.action: Contributors submit improved algorithms.
Miners select and run algorithms to solve challenge instances.
effects: algorithm adoption and performance become observable

steps.action: Calculate influence and distribute rewards under protocol rules.
effects: solvers and algorithm contributors can be compensated

architecture_patterns.name: Proof-of-work security-budget review
architecture_patterns.description: Assess whether the resources securing a network remain adequate relative to plausible attack resources and economic incentives.

steps.action: Estimate honest network hash rate and its concentration.
Estimate the cost and availability of acquiring attack hash power.
Review subsidy, fees, energy costs, hardware access and pool concentration.
Model reorganization, censorship and double-spend consequences.
Reassess after reward changes, halvings or market shifts.
effects: security assumptions are revisited over time

architecture_patterns.name: Energy-aware and interruptible mining operations
architecture_patterns.description: Where market and grid conditions permit, treat mining as a controllable load while evaluating energy source and external costs.

steps.action: Measure electricity use and the energy supply mix.
Identify contractual and technical ability to curtail load.
Respond to grid or market signals where safe and permitted.
Report environmental assumptions and limitations transparently.
effects: externalities are not hidden behind simple energy-price comparisons

architecture_patterns.name: PoW client puzzle for abusive request control
architecture_patterns.description: Use adaptive challenge difficulty to raise the cost of abusive high-volume requests while keeping legitimate traffic usable.

steps.action: Observe service load and abuse indicators.
effects: current risk and capacity are assessed

steps.action: Issue a challenge with a policy-selected difficulty.
effects: requester must perform bounded or probabilistic work

steps.action: Verify the response cheaply.
effects: valid proof can be checked with low server effort

steps.action: Combine PoW with conventional abuse controls and accessibility safeguards.
effects: PoW is not treated as a complete standalone defense

architecture_patterns.name: Chain reorganization response
architecture_patterns.description: Handle competing chain history by applying protocol rules consistently and treating transaction reversals as a risk requiring operational awareness.

steps.action: Detect that a competing chain conflicts with previously accepted blocks.
Validate competing blocks and their proof under consensus rules.
Follow the protocol's canonical-chain selection rule.
effects: nodes converge on the accepted chain under normal assumptions

steps.action: Notify affected services about transactions removed or replaced by the reorganization.

derived_rules.title: Proof generation should be costly relative to verification
derived_rules.statement: A PoW design should document the prover's expected work factor and verifier's validation cost; a high prover cost without cheap reliable verification defeats the core asymmetry.

derived_rules.title: Difficulty controls expected work, not the meaning of the result
derived_rules.statement: Difficulty should be selected for the threat model and service context; satisfying a target proves compliance with that target, not that arbitrary useful work was performed.

derived_rules.title: Interactive challenges can adapt to service load
derived_rules.statement: Where challenge-response is used, adapt difficulty carefully so abuse becomes expensive without making legitimate requests impractical.

derived_rules.title: Bind anti-spam work to the request context
derived_rules.statement: A Hashcash-style stamp should be checked against its specified fields and policy to reduce trivial replay or cross-context reuse.

derived_rules.title: Nodes must independently validate candidate blocks
derived_rules.statement: A miner's claim is not sufficient; nodes must verify proof validity, transactions and consensus rules before accepting a block.

derived_rules.title: Confirmations increase confidence but are not absolute finality
derived_rules.statement: Operational payment policies should account for value and reorganization risk rather than treating any fixed confirmation count as impossible to reverse.

derived_rules.title: Majority hash power can reorganize history
derived_rules.statement: Threat models should include reorganization, double spending and censorship when an attacker controls a majority of relevant mining power.

derived_rules.title: Monitor miner revenue as a security input
derived_rules.statement: Track subsidy and fees alongside hash rate, energy and hardware economics; lower rewards can alter the cost of attacking the network.

derived_rules.title: Measure mining concentration, not only total hash rate
derived_rules.statement: Total network hash rate does not by itself reveal how mining power is coordinated or controlled; monitor pools and ownership concentration.

derived_rules.title: ASIC resistance is not equivalent to attack resistance
derived_rules.statement: Commodity-hardware designs may lower specialization advantages while making large amounts of rentable general-purpose compute relevant to attack analysis.

derived_rules.title: Report energy consumption with context
derived_rules.statement: Energy assessments should state the measurement period, energy mix, system boundary and assumptions; electricity use alone does not settle all environmental or grid questions.

derived_rules.title: Useful-work consensus requires verifiable task outputs
derived_rules.statement: PoUW needs task definitions and solution checks that are compatible with decentralized validation and the consensus security model.

derived_rules.title: Specify reward attribution for algorithm contributions
derived_rules.statement: OPoW-style systems need transparent influence and reward rules so miners and algorithm contributors can understand how adoption affects compensation.

derived_rules.title: Memory-bound work shifts rather than eliminates hardware economics
derived_rules.statement: Memory-intensive algorithms can alter hardware advantages, but implementation, memory bandwidth, ASIC development and access to hardware still require analysis.

derived_rules.title: Treat article-specific statistics and estimates as source-reported
derived_rules.statement: Time-bound attack-cost estimates, energy estimates, policy status and adoption statistics should be revalidated before operational or financial decisions.

derived_rules.title: PoW should not be treated as a complete DoS defense
derived_rules.statement: Computational puzzles can raise abuse cost but should be evaluated alongside rate limits, authentication, queueing and accessibility constraints.

derived_rules.title: Network value does not itself guarantee adequate security expenditure
derived_rules.statement: Compare the resources protecting a network with plausible attack costs; a large market capitalization alone does not establish that history is expensive to rewrite.

derived_rules.title: Difficulty adjustment must be deterministic across compliant nodes
derived_rules.statement: Every node should apply the same protocol rules and input window when deriving the updated target to avoid consensus divergence.

value.source_scope: Structured primarily from the user-supplied Public-key cryptography article text. Descriptions normalize terminology for machine readability; time-sensitive deployment or security claims should be checked against current standards.

value.name: Hybrid encryption and session protection
value.description: Use public-key key establishment or encapsulation to derive a shared secret, then derive a symmetric session key and protect bulk traffic symmetrically.

value.name: PKI-authenticated TLS
value.description: A client validates a certificate chain and identity, authenticates the server public key, performs key establishment, and uses symmetric traffic protection.

value.name: Web-of-trust public-key authentication
value.description: Users use endorsements and key identity checks rather than relying solely on a centralized certificate hierarchy.

value.name: Signed software update
value.description: Publisher signs release metadata or package; client verifies the signature with an authenticated publisher public key before installation.

value.name: Ephemeral key agreement with forward secrecy
value.description: A protocol uses fresh ephemeral key material and erases it appropriately so later compromise of a long-term key need not reveal prior session secrets.

value.name: Public-key trust and revocation lifecycle
value.description: Generate keys securely, bind public keys to identities, validate certificates and status, rotate or revoke compromised credentials, and maintain trust anchors.

value.name: Encrypted content with metadata exposure
value.description: Public-key encryption protects message body content but headers and traffic patterns can remain observable; metadata protection requires additional design.

value.rule: Never treat a received public key as authentic solely because it is available; bind it to the intended identity through a trusted validation method.
value.rationale: Key substitution can enable man-in-the-middle attacks.

value.rule: Protect private keys against disclosure, unauthorized use, backup exposure, and weak custody arrangements.
value.rationale: Anyone with the private key may impersonate its owner or decrypt data depending on the key's role.

value.rule: Use public-key operations for key establishment or encapsulation and symmetric authenticated encryption for bulk data when appropriate.
value.rationale: Public-key operations are generally more computationally expensive than symmetric protection.

value.rule: Validate certificate chain, intended identity, validity period, and revocation status before relying on a certified key.
value.rationale: A compromised or mis-issued certificate authority can undermine the trust hierarchy.

value.rule: Use well-designed ephemeral key agreement and erase ephemeral secrets when forward secrecy is required.
value.rationale: Ephemeral session keys can limit the consequences of later long-term key compromise.

value.rule: Choose algorithms and parameters based on current cryptographic guidance, threat models, and required security lifetime.
value.rationale: Long keys do not repair every algorithmic weakness; some schemes have structural attacks or quantum-related risks.

value.rule: Use constant-time operations and implementation-specific mitigations where relevant; assess side-channel exposure.
value.rationale: Information leakage can compromise keys even when the mathematical algorithm is sound.

value.rule: Do not assume encryption hides sender, recipient, timing, size, subject, or traffic relationships; add metadata protection when required.
value.rationale: Traffic analysis can infer sensitive relationships from unencrypted metadata.

value.rule: Do not confuse digital signatures with encryption: signatures support authenticity/integrity, while encryption protects confidentiality.
value.rationale: A signature does not inherently conceal message content and encryption alone does not authenticate the sender.

value.rule: Use role-appropriate keys and lifecycle policies; consider separating signing keys from encryption/key-agreement keys.
value.rationale: Different operations have different legal, recovery, revocation and forward-secrecy implications.

value.rule: Generate keys and cryptographic randomness with a suitable cryptographically secure random-number generator.
value.rationale: Predictable key material can defeat otherwise sound algorithms.

value.rule: Treat forward secrecy as a protocol property with assumptions, not as a universal guarantee; endpoint compromise and poor ephemeral-secret handling remain risks.
value.rationale: Security depends on protocol implementation and secret erasure.

value.rule: Treat encrypted-header designs as specialized and deployment-dependent rather than assuming metadata privacy is provided by ordinary public-key encryption.
value.rationale: The source describes encrypted metadata as experimental and not broadly deployed at the time of the article.

value.name: Alice signs a message for Bob
steps: Alice signs message data using her private signing key.
Bob obtains an authentic copy of Alice's public key.
Bob verifies the signature against the message.
A valid signature supports integrity and key-possession-based attribution, but does not encrypt the message.

value.name: Source sends an encrypted message to a journalist
steps: The journalist publishes an authentic encryption public key.
The source encrypts the message using that public key.
The journalist decrypts using the paired private key.
Message content is concealed, but ordinary encryption may leave communication metadata visible and does not by itself authenticate the sender.

value.name: Publisher-signed software update
steps: Publisher creates a signing key pair and distributes the public key through a trusted channel or software installation.
Publisher signs an update or its authenticated digest/manifest.
Client verifies the signature before applying the update.
Compromise of the signing key or trust bootstrap can undermine the workflow.

value.name: TLS hybrid cryptosystem
steps: Client authenticates the server certificate and public-key identity.
Protocol establishes or derives shared traffic secrets using public-key cryptographic mechanisms.
Key derivation creates traffic keys.
Symmetric cryptography protects application data; suitable ephemeral key exchange can provide forward secrecy.

value.name: Public-key substitution attack
steps: Attacker intercepts a public-key distribution exchange.
Attacker substitutes a key they control and relays traffic between parties.
Without authenticated key binding, each party may encrypt to or trust the attacker's key.
Certificate validation, web-of-trust checks, or another authenticated channel can prevent or detect substitution.

Message content is concealed, but ordinary encryption may leave communication metadata visible and does not by itself authenticate the sender.

examples.name: Publisher-signed software update
steps: Publisher creates a signing key pair and distributes the public key through a trusted channel or software installation.
Publisher signs an update or its authenticated digest/manifest.
Client verifies the signature before applying the update.
Compromise of the signing key or trust bootstrap can undermine the workflow.

examples.name: TLS hybrid cryptosystem
steps: Client authenticates the server certificate and public-key identity.
Protocol establishes or derives shared traffic secrets using public-key cryptographic mechanisms.
Key derivation creates traffic keys.
Symmetric cryptography protects application data; suitable ephemeral key exchange can provide forward secrecy.

examples.name: Public-key substitution attack
steps: Attacker intercepts a public-key distribution exchange.
Attacker substitutes a key they control and relays traffic between parties.
Without authenticated key binding, each party may encrypt to or trust the attacker's key.
Certificate validation, web-of-trust checks, or another authenticated channel can prevent or detect substitution.
